chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order. Dot plots turn the mean into a balance point, and every change to the data (a new value, a missing value, every value shifted or doubled) is predicted first and then checked. The second half moves from numbers to pictures: line graphs, an infographic and colour strips, each read with the same two questions, what is given and what does it say.

points.text: Each idea opens with a question the student answers before the video reveals it: will the mean go up or down, which dot is missing, which season is wet. The tool then lets the student test the guess.
points.title: Predict, then check

points.text: Every topic has one tool, and no tool is used twice. A tool appears only where handling the data is the concept itself.
points.title: One tool, one idea

points.text: Step one: what is given (axes, scale, marks, who collected it and how). Step two: what can be inferred, and what cannot. Graph values are read approximately and said so.
points.title: Read a graph in two steps

points.text: The chapter closes on projects: strips of the student's own day, sleep logs and school timings, because looking at data leads to new questions.
points.title: Ask your own questions

topics.summary: Two numbers, their mean, and the question that drives the chapter: where is the centre of some data?

content.text:
5.1 The Balancing Act
Last year, we learnt about the mean and median. Recall that the mean of some data is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values in the data. The median is the middle value when the data is sorted.
We shall try to understand the mean and median from a different perspective and see how the mean behaves with changing data.
Consider any 2 numbers. Find their average/arithmetic mean. Repeat this by taking other pairs. What do you observe?
For example, let the two numbers be 3 and 7. Their average is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. Taking another pair of numbers, say 8 and 9, their average is (8 + 9) ÷ 2 = 8.5. Visualising these as dot plots we get the picture. Notice that the mean is exactly halfway between the two numbers.

content.text:
1. Predict first: put a dot on 3 and a dot on 7 on a number line. Where would you put a finger so the two dots balance?
2. The mean of 3 and 7 is 5, exactly halfway. For 8 and 9 it is 8.5, again halfway.
3. For two numbers the mean is the centre. Is that still true when there are three numbers, or four?

media.title: Data Explorer: Balance and Change
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, The Balancing Act: Mean and Median). Add, remove and move dots. Watch the mean keep the balance! Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student sees a dot plot lying on a number line like a plank on a see-saw. The first card shows dots at 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13, with a movable triangle under the line that marks the balance point. Two read-outs hang above the plot, one for the total distance from the triangle to the dots on its left and one for the total on its right. Beside the plot are an Add a value button and a transform panel with plus k, minus k and times k.

Before touching anything the student predicts where the triangle must sit for the plank to stay level, then drags it. The plank tilts towards the heavier side and the totals change as the triangle moves: at 6 they read 4 and 9, at 8 they read 10 and 5, and at 7 both read 7, so the plank levels and turns green. A faint marker at 8, halfway between the end dots 3 and 13, shows that the mean is not the midpoint of the extremes. Every other spot unbalances the plank, so the student sees there is only one centre.

Six cards follow, each asking for a prediction first. The student checks that the two totals are equal at the mean 7. Then a dot at 10 is added and the triangle slides to 7.5, so the student says the mean rises. A dot added exactly on the triangle changes nothing, and both totals grow by zero. With plus k set to 4 every dot slides 4 to the right together and the triangle goes with them, so the student predicts 11 and sees the old mean plus 4 written beside it. With times 3 the dots spread out to 9, 15, 18, 24 and 39, and the student predicts 21. The last card asks the student to drag one dot so that the mean becomes 8, and the triangle follows the dot live. A wrong prediction shows the two distance totals so the student sees which side is heavier. The student may also add a pair of values, one 4 below the mean and one 4 above, here 3 and 11, and see the mean stay at 7.

Hints go in order: where would a see-saw under the dots have to sit to stay level? Then: compare the total distance on the left with the total on the right. Then: a value added above the mean makes the left side longer, so the balance point moves right. Last, the value is shown with both totals and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the mean is the one point where the distances on the two sides are equal, that a value above it pulls it up, one below pulls it down and one equal to it leaves it, and that shifting or scaling every value shifts or scales the mean in the same way.

topics.summary: The mean balances the distances on both sides, a new value above it pulls it up, a value below pulls it down, adding k to every value adds k to the mean, and multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean by k.

content.text:
Calculate and mark the mean of each collection of data below.
Can you explain how the mean is the centre of each collection?
Is the mean the midpoint of the two endpoints/extremes of the data? It is not always so. Instead, the total distances are equal on both the sides of the mean.
Verify that this holds for all the collections of data shown earlier.
Can there be more than one such centre? In other words, is there any other value such that the sum of the distances to the values lower than it and the values higher than it will still be equal?
In the case of the collection 10, 10, 11, and 17 whose mean is 12, suppose there is a different centre larger than 12. Clearly, all the distances on the LHS will increase and the distances on the RHS will decrease. Thus, it is no longer the centre. Similarly, for any value smaller than 12, the distances on the LHS will decrease while those on the RHS will increase.
Therefore, there is only one centre.

Can there be more than one such centre? In other words, is there any other value such that the sum of the distances to the values lower than it and the values higher than it will still be equal?

In the case of the collection 10, 10, 11, and 17 whose mean is 12, suppose there is a different centre larger than 12. Clearly, all the distances on the LHS will increase and the distances on the RHS will decrease. Thus, it is no longer the centre. Similarly, for any value smaller than 12, the distances on the LHS will decrease while those on the RHS will increase.

Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 5): Check whether each statement is true and justify it, using algebra if needed: (i) The average of two even numbers is even. (ii) The average of any two multiples of 5 is a multiple of 5. (iii) The average of any 5 multiples of 5 is also a multiple of 5.
1. (i) Write the numbers as 2a and 2b. Their average is a + b, which can be odd. 2 and 4 give 3. False.
2. (ii) Write them as 5a and 5b. The average is 5(a + b) ÷ 2, which is not always a multiple of 5. 5 and 10 give 7.5. False.
3. (iii) The average of 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e is a + b + c + d + e, which need not be a multiple of 5. 5, 5, 5, 5, 10 give 6. False.
Answer: All three statements are false

content.question: Use algebra to show what happens to the mean when 2 is subtracted from every one of n values whose mean is a.
content.text: Use algebra to show what happens to the mean when $2$ is subtracted from every one of $n$ values whose mean is a.

content.question_tex: Use algebra to show what happens to the mean when $2$ is subtracted from every one of $n$ values whose mean is a.

concepts.concept_name: The Balancing Act: How the Mean Changes: Ans2

steps: The values are x1, x2, … xn, and (x1 + x2 + … + xn) ÷ n = a.
The new sum is (x1 − 2) + (x2 − 2) + … + (xn − 2) = x1 + x2 + … + xn − 2n.
Dividing by n gives a − 2.
content.answer: The new mean is a − 2

$1$. The values are $x1$, $x2$, … $xn$, and $(x1 + x2 + \ldots + xn) \div n = a$.

$3$. Dividing by $n$ gives $a - 2$.
Answer: The new mean is $a - 2$

content.question: Find the mean of the following data and share your observations: (i) The first 50 natural numbers. (ii) The first 50 odd numbers. (iii) The first 50 multiples of 4.
content.text: Find the mean of the following data and share your observations: (i): The first $50$ natural numbers. (ii): The first $50$ odd numbers. (iii): The first $50$ multiples of $4$.

content.question_tex: Find the mean of the following data and share your observations: (i): The first $50$ natural numbers. (ii): The first $50$ odd numbers. (iii): The first $50$ multiples of $4$.

concepts.concept_name: The Balancing Act: How the Mean Changes: Ans3

steps: (i) The sum is 50 × 51 ÷ 2 = 1275, so the mean is 1275 ÷ 50 = 25.5.
(ii) The first 50 odd numbers add to 50 × 50 = 2500, so the mean is 2500 ÷ 50 = 50.
(iii) These are 4 times the natural numbers, so the mean is 4 × 25.5 = 102.
Observation: for evenly spaced values the mean is the average of the first and the last value.

media.description: Leeza measures the heights of all twenty four students and finds an average of one hundred and fifty point two centimetres, but the uniform shoes add one centimetre to every height. media.title: Can a grid of nine numbers have average 10 in every line?

media.description: A question from the book asks for a three by three grid of nine different numbers in which every row, column and diagonal has an average of ten. The video turns the average into a line total, builds a grid by shifting every number of a known grid, and then changes some numbers to get another grid.

media.title: Are these three statements about averages always true?

media.description: A question from the book gives three statements about the average of two even numbers, of two multiples of five, and of five multiples of five. The video writes each kind of number with a letter, finds the average with algebra, and checks each statement with numbers.

video_script.why: The child cannot settle an always-true claim by trying a few numbers, so the video writes the numbers with letters and finds the average.

<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each statement always true?

media.title: Missing Value Lab: Mean and Median
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, The Balancing Act: Mean and Median). Find a hidden value from the mean. Then watch how the median reacts! Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.tool_name: Missing Value Lab: Mean and Median
media.description:
A row of value cards runs across the top of the screen, and one card is smudged into an ink blot. Above it a switch chooses Mean or Median, and a target line states the given mean or median and how many values there are. Below the row sit a running total and a sorted order strip that is used in median mode.

In Mean mode the student first says what the target tells about the total. Card 1 has four wrestlers who weigh 40, 42, 44 and one smudged weight, with a mean of 43. The student writes the total, 4 times 43 equals 172, then types a weight into the blot and watches the running total move. A wrong try such as 44 shows a total of 170 and a mean of 42.5 beside the target 43. The right weight, 46, locks, and the rule appears: 172 minus the known 126 gives 46. Card 2 is a coconut harvest of 15 trees with a mean of 25.6 but no list of counts. The cards are replaced by one total bar. The student finds 25.6 times 15 equals 384, takes off the 3 that was counted too many to reach 381, and divides by 15 to get the corrected mean 25.4, a drop of 0.2, which is the 3 shared over 15 trees. Card 3 gives five numbers with mean 12 and four known, for example 9, 11, 14 and 15. The total must be 60, the known ones make 49, and the blank is 11.

In Median mode the sorted strip does the work. Card 4 shows 9, 12, 15, 20 and a blank, with a median of 15. As the student drags values into the blank, the five cards re-sort and the middle card lights up. A 10 leaves 12 in the middle, 13 puts 13 there, and 15 or any larger value puts 15 there, so the student finds that the blank can be anything from 15 upwards. Card 5 uses the set 9, 12, 15, 17, 20 and asks for a value that keeps the median at 15. Adding 15 works, the middle two both being 15, while 11 drops the median to 13.5 and 25 lifts it to 16. Card 6 asks for two values that raise the median. Adding 25 and 30 gives 17, but adding 5 and 25 leaves it at 15, because one value below cancels one above.

Hints go in order: what does the mean tell you about the total of all the values? Then: find the target total, then subtract the values you already have. Then: total needed minus the sum of the known values is the missing value. Last, the missing value is shown with its working and a similar card follows. The student states the rule in words at the end of each mode. Through doing, the student learns that a known mean fixes the total, so a missing value is the total minus the known values, and that a known median fixes the middle position, so ordering the values shows what the missing one must satisfy.

topics.summary: A value above the median pulls it up, one below pulls it down, and a given mean gives the total, so one missing value or one correction can be worked out.

content.text:
We know that the median is the middle value in the sorted data: there are an equal number of values less than it and greater than it.
Will including a new value to the data increase or decrease the median? Let us consider the following data. The median of this data is 8.
Suppose we include a value 11. The new value included is greater than the (earlier) median: the median can no longer be 8 as there are more values greater than it. Therefore, the median will also increase. The median, now, will be the average of the two middle values 8 and 11, which is 9.5.
We can similarly argue that when a value less than the median is included, the median will decrease.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the median of the data is 8. Include 11. Does the median move up, down, or stay?
2. 11 is above the median, so more values now sit above 8 than below it. The middle shifts up. The two middle values are now 8 and 11, and the median is 9.5.
3. A value below the median moves the middle down. Removing a value works the other way round.

Worked example: A data set has median 8 and its two middle values after including 11 are 8 and 11. Find the new median.
1. The new median is the average of the two middle values 8 and 11.
2. (8 + 11) ÷ 2 = 19 ÷ 2 = 9.5.
3. 9.5 is above 8, so the median rose, as predicted.

content.text:
Coach Balwan noted down the weights of the kushti players (wrestlers) and the mean as shown. But one value that was written down got smudged. Can you find out the missing value?
Average weight of the players = Sum of weight of all players ÷ Number of players.
Let the unknown weight be w kg. (42 + 40 + 39 + 33 + 48 + 38 + 42 + 35 + 32 + w) ÷ 10 = 39.2. Simplifying this we get, 349 + w = 392, w = 392 − 349 = 43. The missing value is 43 kg.

Average weight of the players = Sum of weight of all players ÷ Number of players.
Let the unknown weight be w kg. (42 + 40 + 39 + 33 + 48 + 38 + 42 + 35 + 32 + w) ÷ 10 = 39.2. Simplifying this we get, 349 + w = 392, w = 392 − 349 = 43. The missing value is 43 kg.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the mean of 10 weights is 39.2. Without knowing the 10th weight, what can you already say about the total?
2. Mean times the number of players is the total: 39.2 × 10 = 392.
3. The nine known weights add to 349. So the missing weight is 392 − 349 = 43 kg.

Venkayya keeps track of the coconut harvest in his farm. He calculates the average harvest per tree as 25.6. His son verifies the counts and finds that one tree's harvest count is incorrectly noted as 3 more than the actual number. Can you find the correct average if the number of trees is 15?
The data of harvest per tree is not given. Can we still find out the number of coconuts harvested?
z ÷ 15 = 25.6, so z = 25.6 × 15 = 384. The actual total harvest count is 384 − 3 = 381. The correct average harvest is 381 ÷ 15 = 25.4.

Figure it Out (mean and median, question 6): Justify whether each statement is always true, sometimes true or never true: (i) Removing a value less than the median will decrease the median. (ii) Including a value less than the mean will decrease the mean. (iii) Including any 4 values will not affect the median. (iv) Including 4 values less than the median will increase the median.
1. (i) Never true. The middle moves up or stays; for 1, 2, 3 removing 1 gives 2 and 3 with median 2.5.
2. (ii) Always true. A value below the mean adds more left distance, so the balance point moves down.
3. (iii) Sometimes true. Two low and two high values leave it; four high values do not.
4. (iv) Never true. Values below the median push it down or leave it.
Answer: (i) never (ii) always (iii) sometimes (iv) never

content.text:
Figure it Out (mean and median, question 9): Consider the data 12, 47, 8, 73, 18, 35, 39, 8, 29, 25, p. Which of these could be p if the median is 29? (i) 10 (ii) 25 (iii) 40 (iv) 100 (v) 29 (vi) 47 (vii) 30
1. With p there are 11 values, so the median is the 6th value when sorted.
2. Without p the sorted values are 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, 35, 39, 47, 73.
3. If p is below 29 the 6th value drops to 25 at most, so p must be at least 29.
4. For p at least 29 the five values below stay 8, 8, 12, 18, 25 and the 6th is 29.
Answer: p could be 40, 100, 29, 47 or 30, that is (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii)

Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 3): Fill in the blanks so the median is 13: 5, 21, 14, _, _, _. How many possibilities exist if only counting numbers are allowed?
1. With 6 values the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th, so they must add to 26.
2. For example 1, 12, 14 gives 1, 5, 12, 14, 14, 21 with middle values 12 and 14.
3. Also 12, 13, 13 gives 5, 12, 13, 13, 14, 21, and 3, 12, 100 works.
4. One blank can be made as large as we like, so the possibilities never end.
Answer: For example 1, 12, 14; there are infinitely many possibilities

content.text:
Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 6): Two new students join a class whose average height was 150.2 cm with 24 students. (i) Which statements are correct? (ii) The new heights are 149 cm and 152 cm: what happens to the mean? (iii) What happens to the median?
1. (i) The new heights have to be measured, since they decide the new average. The others claim too much.
2. (ii) 149 is 1.2 below 150.2 and 152 is 1.8 above. The surplus wins, so the average increases slightly: (24 × 150.2 + 149 + 152) ÷ 26 ≈ 150.22.
3. (iii) The median depends on the actual heights, which we are not given, so there is not enough information.
Answer: (i) the new heights must be measured (ii) the average increases (iii) not enough information

2. The median depends on who the three people are and where they sit in the sorted list, so we cannot say.
Answer: The mean is unchanged; nothing can be said about the median

content.question: Coach Balwan's mean weight of 10 players is 39.2 kg. Nine weights are 42, 40, 39, 33, 48, 38, 42, 35 and 32 kg. Find the smudged weight.
content.book_number: Example 1: Finding the Unknown: Coach Balwan's smudged weight
content.text:
$1$. The nine known weights add to $42 + 40 + 39 + 33 + 48 + 38 + 42 + 35 + 32 = 349$.
$2$. Let the missing weight be $w$. Then $(349 + w) \div 10 = 39.2$.
$3$. $349 + w = 39.2 \times 10 = 392$.
$4$. $w = 392 - 349 = 43$.
Answer: The missing weight is $43\text{ kg}$

content.question: Find the median of 8, 10, 19, 23, 26, 34, 40, 41, 41, 48, 51, 55, 70, 84, 91, 92. (i) What value can be included without affecting the median? (ii) What two values? (iii) What one value can be removed without affecting the median?

content.question_tex: Find the median of $8$, $10$, $19$, $23$, $26$, $34$, $40$, $41$, $41$, $48$, $51$, $55$, $70$, $84$, $91$, $92$. (i): What value can be included without affecting the median? (ii): What two values? (iii): What one value can be removed without affecting the median?

concepts.concept_name: Tinkering with the Median and Finding the Unknown: Ans1

steps: There are 16 values, so the median is the average of the 8th and 9th values 41 and 41, which is 41.
(i) Include 41. The middle value stays 41.
(ii) Include one value at most 41 and one at least 41, for example 10 and 90.
(iii) Remove one of the two 41s. The 15 values left have the 8th value as 41.
content.answer: The median is 41; add 41; add a pair like 10 and 90; remove a 41

content.text:
$1$. There are $16$ values, so the median is the average of the $8\text{th}$ and $9\text{th}$ values $41$ and $41$, which is $41$.
$2$. (i): Include $41$. The middle value stays $41$.
$3$. (ii): Include one value at most $41$ and one at least $41$, for example $10$ and $90$.
$4$. (iii): Remove one of the two $41s$. The $15$ values left have the $8\text{th}$ value as $41$.
Answer: The median is $41$; add $41$; add a pair like $10$ and $90$; remove a $41$

media.title: Are these four statements about mean and median always true?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Four statements about removing or including values are tested on small lists. Each is judged to be always true, sometimes true or never true, with a reason from where the middle value or the balance point moves.

video_script.why: A child who has seen the median and the mean move when a value is included now judges general statements about them.

marks.ask: the three words always, sometimes, never appear beside the cards
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the median and the mean.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Four statements are given.
The first says removing a value less than the median will decrease the median.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second says including a value less than the mean will decrease the mean.
<bookmark mark='third'/>The third says including any four values will not affect the median.
<bookmark mark='fourth'/>The fourth says including four values less than the median will increase the median.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is each one always true, sometimes true, or never true?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; four statement cards about median and mean, each with an empty box for always, sometimes or never

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the four statement cards and the question stay on the board

marks.some: a tick and a cross appear under sometimes true
marks.never: a cross appears for every list under never true
marks.small: a small list of dots 1, 2, 3 appears
marks.always: a tick appears for every list under always true

narration: <bookmark mark='always'/>Always true means the statement holds for every list.
<bookmark mark='some'/>Sometimes true means it holds for some lists and fails for others.
<bookmark mark='never'/>Never true means it fails for every list.
<bookmark mark='small'/>We test each statement on small lists and look for a reason.
beats.on_screen: always true: holds for every list; sometimes true: holds for some lists; never true: fails for every list; test on small lists

marks.given: the four statements are listed

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, four statements about the median and the mean.
beats.on_screen: Given: four statements about the median and the mean

marks.find: the words always, sometimes, never are written with a reason line

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to judge each statement and give a reason.
beats.on_screen: To find: always, sometimes or never true, with a reason for each

marks.up: an up arrow appears beside the marker
marks.why: the words never true are written
marks.list: the list 1, 2, 3 appears with the median 2 marked
marks.remove: the dot at 1 is removed and the marker moves to 2.5

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step one, test the first statement with one, two and three.
The median is two.
<bookmark mark='remove'/>Remove one, which is less than the median.
Two and three are left, and the median is two point five.
<bookmark mark='up'/>The median went up, not down.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Taking out a low value pushes the middle up or leaves it.
The first statement is never true.
beats.on_screen: first: 1, 2, 3 has median 2; remove 1: 2, 3 has median 2.5, which is up, not down

marks.why: the words always true are written
marks.join: a dot at 2 joins and the balance marker moves to 4
marks.list: the list 4, 6 appears with the mean 5 marked

narration: <bookmark mark='list'/>Step two, test the second statement.
Four and six have a mean of five.
<bookmark mark='join'/>Include two, which is less than the mean.
Four, six and two have a mean of four.
<bookmark mark='why'/>The mean went down.
A value below the mean always pulls the mean down, so the second statement is always true.
beats.on_screen: second: 4, 6 has mean 5; include 2: (4 + 6 + 2) ÷ 3 = 4, which is down

marks.low: the list 1, 2, 3 appears with the median 2 marked
marks.high: 10, 10, 10, 10 join the list 1, 2, 3 and the median jumps to 10
marks.some: the words sometimes true are written
marks.zeros: 0, 0, 10, 10 join the list and the median stays at 2

narration: <bookmark mark='low'/>Step three, test the third statement two ways.
Take one, two and three, with median two.
<bookmark mark='zeros'/>Include zero, zero, ten and ten, and the median is still two.
<bookmark mark='high'/>Include ten, ten, ten and ten instead, and the median becomes ten.
<bookmark mark='some'/>It holds for some choices and fails for others, so the third statement is sometimes true.
beats.on_screen: third: 1, 2, 3 plus 0, 0, 10, 10 has median 2, unchanged; 1, 2, 3 plus 10, 10, 10, 10 has median 10, changed

marks.why: the words never true are written
marks.zeros: four dots at 0 join the list 1, 2, 3

narration: <bookmark mark='zeros'/>Step four, test the fourth statement.
Take one, two and three, and include four zeros.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>The sorted list has seven values, and the middle one is zero.
The median went down from two to zero.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Values below the median never push it up, so the fourth statement is never true.
beats.on_screen: fourth: 1, 2, 3 plus 0, 0, 0, 0 sorted is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3 with median 0, which is down

marks.fall: four zeros join and the marker falls to 1
marks.second: the list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 appears with the median 3 marked

narration: <bookmark mark='second'/>Check the fourth statement with a second list.
One, two, three, four, five has a median of three.
<bookmark mark='fall'/>Include four zeros, and the fifth of nine values is one.
The median fell again.
beats.on_screen: check: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 has median 3; plus 0, 0, 0, 0 the 5th of 9 values is 1, so the median fell

marks.ans: the four judgements are boxed in order

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The answers are never, always, sometimes and never.
beats.on_screen: Answer: never, always, sometimes, never

video_script.anchor: a small row of dots 1, 2, 3 with the median marked and the mean as a balance point
video_script.design: One row of dots all video. For each statement a test list is built from the same dots, one value is removed or included, and the median marker or the balance point is watched.
source: Figure it Out (mean and median, question 6)
never_show: a statement marked always true from one example alone
maths_rules: (i) 1, 2, 3 has median 2; removing 1 leaves 2, 3 with median 2.5; removing a value below the median moves the median up or leaves it, so never true
(ii) 4, 6 has mean 5; including 2 gives total 12 over 3 values, mean 4; a value below the mean always lowers the mean, so always true
(iii) 1, 2, 3 plus 0, 0, 10, 10 sorted is 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 10 with median 2 (unchanged); 1, 2, 3 plus 10, 10, 10, 10 sorted is 1, 2, 3, 10, 10, 10, 10 with median 10 (changed); so sometimes true
(iv) 1, 2, 3 plus four 0s sorted is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3 with median 0 (lower, not higher); values below the median never raise it, so never true
check: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 has median 3; plus four 0s sorted is 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the 5th value is 1, so the median fell from 3 to 1
video_script.payoff_line: The answers are never, always, sometimes and never

final_answer.value: never, always, sometimes, never
final_answer.spoken: the answers are never, always, sometimes and never

video_script.substitution: the book's four statements, tested on the small list 1, 2, 3 and a second list

media.teaching_notes: One idea: one small list can show a statement is not always true, and a reason about the middle or the balance point shows it is always or never true. Watch for students who call a statement always true after checking only one example.

interaction_points.answer: never, always, sometimes, never

media.title: How can a mean reveal a hidden number in a list?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Eight numbers have a mean of ten point three seven five, and one of them is hidden as y. The mean gives the total of all eight, and taking away the seven known numbers leaves the hidden one.

video_script.why: A child who has found a smudged weight from a mean now finds a letter value from a mean.

marks.ask: a question mark glows over the box marked y
marks.row: the row of eight boxes appears with the seventh box marked y
marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.mean: the words mean 10.375 appear above the row

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Eight numbers are given, and one of them is hidden.
They are eight, thirteen, ten, four, five, twenty, the hidden number, and ten.
<bookmark mark='mean'/>Their mean is ten point three seven five, and the book asks for the hidden number.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What could it be?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a row of eight boxes holding 8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10; the mean 10.375 above the row

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the row of boxes and the question stay on the board

marks.left: the known boxes are grouped, with the hidden box left on its own
marks.rule: the line mean = total ÷ count appears
marks.turn: the line turns around into total = mean × count

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>The mean is the total divided by the count.
<bookmark mark='turn'/>Turn it around, and the total is the mean multiplied by the count.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The hidden number is what is left when the known numbers are taken from the total.
beats.on_screen: mean = total ÷ count; turned around: total = mean × count

marks.given: the eight numbers and the mean are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are eight numbers and the mean is ten point three seven five.
Seven of the numbers are known.

marks.find: the words the value of y are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the hidden number.
beats.on_screen: To find: the value of y

narration: <bookmark mark='times'/>Step one, turn the mean into the total.
Multiply ten point three seven five by eight.
<bookmark mark='total'/>Ten times eight is eighty, and nought point three seven five times eight is three.
The total is eighty three.

marks.add: the seven known numbers are added one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step two, add the seven known numbers.
Eight, thirteen, ten, four, five, twenty and ten.
<bookmark mark='known'/>Their sum is seventy, which is the total of the known part.

marks.take: 70 is taken away from 83 and y is left

narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step three, take the known sum away from the total.
Eighty three take away seventy leaves thirteen.

marks.back: 13 goes back into the hidden box
marks.match: 83 ÷ 8 = 10.375 matches the mean in the book

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Check the result.
Put thirteen back, and the eight numbers add up to eighty three.
<bookmark mark='match'/>Eighty three divided by eight is ten point three seven five, the mean in the book.

marks.ans: the hidden box fills and the answer is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The hidden number is thirteen.
beats.on_screen: Answer: y = 13

video_script.anchor: a row of eight boxes holding 8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10 with the mean 10.375 above
video_script.design: One row of eight boxes all video, with the seventh box hidden. The mean turns into a total, the known boxes are added, and the hidden box is filled at the end.
source: Figure it Out (mean and median, question 7)
never_show: 10.375 as the value of y
video_script.payoff_line: The hidden number is thirteen

final_answer.spoken: the hidden number is thirteen

video_script.substitution: the book's eight numbers with the mean 10.375 and the hidden number y

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the mean times the count gives the total, and the total minus the known values gives the missing value. Watch for students who add the known numbers and divide them by eight before using the mean.

media.title: What total does a mean of one hundred thirty four give?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A set of fifteen values has a mean of one hundred and thirty four. The mean shares the total equally, so multiplying the mean by the number of values gives the sum of the data.

video_script.why: A child who can find a mean from a total now turns a mean back into a total.

marks.ask: the words sum of the data appear with an empty box
marks.set: a set of fifteen values appears
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean.
<bookmark mark='set'/>A set of data has fifteen values.
<bookmark mark='mean'/>The mean of the set is one hundred and thirty four.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The book asks for the sum of the data.
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a set of 15 values with the mean 134; the words sum of the data with an empty box

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the set and the question stay on the board

marks.rule: the line total = mean × count appears

narration: <bookmark mark='piles'/>A mean shares the total equally, so picture fifteen equal piles.
<bookmark mark='each'/>Each pile holds the mean, which is one hundred and thirty four.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>All the piles together make the total, which is the mean times the count.
beats.on_screen: a mean shares the total equally: 15 equal piles, each holding 134

marks.given: the number of values and the mean are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, there are fifteen values and the mean is one hundred and thirty four.
beats.on_screen: Given: 15 values; mean = 134

marks.find: the words the sum of the data are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the sum of all fifteen values.
beats.on_screen: To find: the sum of the data

marks.rule: sum = mean × number of values is written

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, use the sum as the mean multiplied by the number of values.
<bookmark mark='put'/>That is one hundred and thirty four times fifteen.
beats.on_screen: sum = mean × number of values = 134 × 15

narration: <bookmark mark='ten'/>Step two, split fifteen into ten and five.
One hundred and thirty four times ten is one thousand three hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='five'/>One hundred and thirty four times five is six hundred and seventy.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Add them, and the total is two thousand and ten.

marks.back: each pile reads 134, the mean in the book
marks.share: 2010 is shared into fifteen equal piles

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Check the result by sharing the total back into fifteen equal piles.
<bookmark mark='back'/>Two thousand and ten divided by fifteen is one hundred and thirty four, the mean we started with.

marks.ans: the answer is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The sum of the data is two thousand and ten.
beats.on_screen: Answer: Sum = 2010

video_script.anchor: fifteen equal piles, each labelled with the mean 134
video_script.design: One set of fifteen equal piles all video, each pile holding the mean. The piles are counted into one big total, and the total is shared back into piles for the check.
source: Figure it Out (mean and median, question 8)
never_show: 134 ÷ 15 as the sum, marked as right
maths_rules: sum = mean × number of values = 134 × 15
video_script.payoff_line: The sum of the data is two thousand and ten

final_answer.spoken: the sum of the data is two thousand and ten

video_script.substitution: the book's set of 15 values with mean 134

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the sum of the data equals the mean times the number of values. Watch for students who divide the mean by the number of values instead.

media.title: Which values can the missing eleventh value be?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Ten values are known and an eleventh value p is missing. The median of all eleven must be twenty nine, which is the sixth value when sorted. Testing where p lands in the sorted list shows which of the seven choices work.

video_script.why: A child who has found a median by sorting now decides where a missing value may sit so that the median stays fixed.

marks.gap: a box marked p appears at the end of the row
marks.ten: the ten known values appear in a row
marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.choices: the seven choices 10, 25, 40, 100, 29, 47, 30 appear in a list

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the median.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Ten values are known.
Twelve, forty seven, eight, seventy three, eighteen, thirty five, thirty nine, eight, twenty nine, twenty five.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>An eleventh value is not known, and the median of all eleven must be twenty nine.
<bookmark mark='choices'/>Which of these can the eleventh value be?
Ten, twenty five, forty, one hundred, twenty nine, forty seven, thirty.
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; the ten values 12, 47, 8, 73, 18, 35, 39, 8, 29, 25 and a box marked p; the words median 29

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the row, the gap and the choices stay on the board

marks.eleven: a row of eleven sorted dots appears

narration: <bookmark mark='eleven'/>With eleven values, the median is the sixth value when they are sorted.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Five values lie below it and five lie above it.

marks.given: the ten known values, the box p and the median are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, ten values are known, one value is missing, and the median of all eleven is twenty nine.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which choices can be the missing value.
beats.on_screen: To find: which choices can be p

marks.sort: the ten known values slide into sorted order

narration: <bookmark mark='sort'/>Step one, sort the ten known values.
Eight, eight, twelve, eighteen, twenty five, twenty nine, thirty five, thirty nine, forty seven, seventy three.
<bookmark mark='six'/>The sixth of these ten values is twenty nine.

marks.high: p drops in at or after the 29 and the 6th place stays 29

narration: <bookmark mark='high'/>Step two, try a missing value that is twenty nine or more.
It goes beside the twenty nine or after it, so the sixth value stays twenty nine.
beats.on_screen: p at least 29: p goes at or after 29, so the 6th value stays 29

marks.low: p drops in before the 29 and 29 slides to 7th place
marks.less: the 6th place now holds a value less than 29

narration: <bookmark mark='low'/>Step three, try a missing value below twenty nine.
It goes before the twenty nine and pushes it to seventh place.
<bookmark mark='less'/>Then the sixth value is below twenty nine, and the median is not twenty nine.
beats.on_screen: p less than 29: p goes before 29, so the 6th value is less than 29

marks.no: 10 and 25 are crossed out as below 29
marks.yes: 40, 100, 29, 47 and 30 get ticks as 29 or more

narration: <bookmark mark='no'/>Step four, sort the choices.
Ten and twenty five are below twenty nine, so they fail.
<bookmark mark='yes'/>Forty, one hundred, twenty nine, forty seven and thirty are twenty nine or more, so they work.
beats.on_screen: sort the choices: below 29: 10, 25 (no); 29 or more: 40, 100, 29, 47, 30 (yes)

marks.fail: twenty five is placed in the row and the 6th dot reads 25
marks.pass: thirty is placed in the row and the 6th dot reads 29

narration: <bookmark mark='pass'/>Check one choice that works and one that fails.
With thirty, the sixth value is still twenty nine.
<bookmark mark='fail'/>With twenty five, the row has two twenty fives.
The sixth value is twenty five, not twenty nine.

marks.ans: the five working choices are boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The value can be forty, one hundred, twenty nine, forty seven or thirty.
beats.on_screen: Answer: p can be 40, 100, 29, 47 or 30

source: Figure it Out (mean and median, question 9)
never_show: 10 or 25 marked as a possible value of p
maths_rules: the ten known values sorted: 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, 35, 39, 47, 73
with p there are 11 values, so the median is the 6th sorted value
if p is at least 29, the six smallest values are 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, so the 6th is 29
if p is less than 29, the six smallest values include p and the 6th is less than 29 (25 when p is at most 25, and p when p is between 25 and 29)
10 and 25 are less than 29, so they fail; 40, 100, 29, 47 and 30 are at least 29, so they work
check: p = 30 gives 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 29, 30, ... with 6th value 29; p = 25 gives 8, 8, 12, 18, 25, 25, 29, ... with 6th value 25

final_answer.spoken: the value can be forty, one hundred, twenty nine, forty seven or thirty

media.title: Can you build lists that meet each mean and median rule?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Five conditions on a mean or a median are each met by two lists of numbers. A mean fixes the total, and a median fixes the middle of the sorted list, so many lists can meet one rule.

video_script.why: A child who can find a missing value from a mean now builds whole lists that meet a mean or median rule.

marks.one: the first two condition cards appear: 3 numbers with mean 8; 4 numbers with median 15.5
marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.four: the last two condition cards appear: 6 numbers with mean equal to median; 6 numbers with mean greater than median
marks.three: the third condition card appears: 5 numbers with mean 13.6

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean and the median.
Give two lists of numbers for each of five conditions.
<bookmark mark='one'/>First, three numbers whose mean is eight.
Second, four numbers whose median is fifteen point five.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Third, five numbers whose mean is thirteen point six.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Fourth, six numbers whose mean equals the median.
Fifth, six numbers whose mean is greater than the median.
What lists would you give?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; five condition cards, each with two empty rows of boxes

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the condition cards and the question stay on the board

marks.mid: the middle of a sorted row is marked, with the other boxes left free
marks.total: the line total = mean × count appears

narration: <bookmark mark='total'/>A mean fixes the total, because the total is the mean times the count.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>A median fixes only the middle of the sorted list, so the other numbers are free to change.
beats.on_screen: a mean fixes the total: total = mean × count; a median fixes only the middle of the sorted list

marks.given: the five conditions are listed

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, five conditions, each about a mean or a median.
beats.on_screen: Given: five conditions on mean and median

marks.find: the words two lists for each condition are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find two lists for each condition.
beats.on_screen: To find: two lists for each condition

narration: <bookmark mark='total'/>Step one, three numbers with a mean of eight need a total of twenty four.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Seven, eight and nine add to twenty four.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Four, eight and twelve also add to twenty four.

marks.mid: the middle pair of four boxes is marked with the total 31

narration: <bookmark mark='mid'/>Step two, four numbers with median fifteen point five.
The middle pair must add to thirty one, because the median is their average.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Take ten, fifteen, sixteen and twenty.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Or take one, fifteen, sixteen and ninety nine.
beats.on_screen: 4 numbers, median 15.5: middle pair adds to 31; 10, 15, 16, 20 and 1, 15, 16, 99

narration: <bookmark mark='total'/>Step three, five numbers with a mean of thirteen point six need a total of sixty eight.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Ten, twelve, thirteen, fifteen and eighteen add to sixty eight.
<bookmark mark='second'/>One, two, three, four and fifty eight also add to sixty eight.

marks.same: a second row of six 5s appears

narration: <bookmark mark='six'/>Step four, take one, two, three, four, five and six.
<bookmark mark='mean'/>The total is twenty one, so the mean is three point five.
<bookmark mark='median'/>The middle pair is three and four, so the median is three point five too.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Six fives work as well, because every number is the same.
beats.on_screen: 6 numbers, mean = median: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 has total 21, mean 3.5, median (3 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3.5; also 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5

marks.big: one large dot pulls the balance point to the right
marks.first: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 7 fill a row with median 1 and mean 2
marks.second: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 60 fill a second row with median 7 and mean 15

narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>Step five, one large number pulls the mean above the median.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Take one, one, one, one, one and seven.
The median is one, and the total is twelve, so the mean is two.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Or take two, four, six, eight, ten and sixty.
The median is seven, and the mean is fifteen.
beats.on_screen: 6 numbers, mean > median: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 7 has median 1 and mean 2; 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 60 has median 7 and mean 15

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Check two of the lists.
Ten, twelve, thirteen, fifteen and eighteen add to sixty eight.
Sixty eight divided by five is thirteen point six.
<bookmark mark='next'/>Four, eight and twelve add to twenty four, and twenty four divided by three is eight.

marks.ans: the ten lists are boxed in pairs

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each condition has two lists that meet it.
beats.on_screen: Answer: both lists work for every condition

video_script.anchor: a row of empty boxes ready to be filled with numbers for each condition
video_script.design: One row of boxes all video. For each condition the boxes are filled twice, and a total tag or a middle-pair tag shows why the list meets the rule.
source: Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 2)
never_show: a list that does not meet its condition, marked as right
maths_rules: (i) 3 numbers, mean 8, total 24: 7 + 8 + 9 = 24 and 4 + 8 + 12 = 24
(ii) 4 numbers, median 15.5, middle pair adds to 31: 10, 15, 16, 20 and 1, 15, 16, 99
(iv) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6: total 21, mean 3.5, median (3 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3.5; and six equal numbers such as 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5
(v) 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 7: median 1, total 12, mean 2; and 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 60: median (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7, total 90, mean 15
video_script.payoff_line: Each condition has two lists that meet it

final_answer.value: two lists for each condition
final_answer.spoken: each condition has two lists that meet it

media.title: How many ways can three blanks give a median of thirteen?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Three blanks follow the numbers five, twenty one and fourteen, and the median of all six must be thirteen. The third and fourth sorted values must add to twenty six, and one blank can grow without end.

video_script.why: A child who finds a median from two middle values now works backwards from the median to fill blanks.

marks.ask: the words how many ways appear with an empty box
marks.row: the row of six boxes appears with 5, 21 and 14 filled and three blanks
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the median.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Six boxes hold five, twenty one, fourteen and three blanks.
<bookmark mark='median'/>Fill the blanks so that the median of all six numbers is thirteen.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many ways are there if only counting numbers are allowed?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a row of six boxes holding 5, 21, 14 and three blanks; the words median 13

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the row of boxes and the question stay on the board

marks.six: six sorted boxes appear with the 3rd and 4th marked

narration: <bookmark mark='six'/>With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth values when sorted.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>A median of thirteen means that those two values add up to twenty six.
beats.on_screen: 6 sorted values: the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th; a median of 13 means 3rd + 4th = 26

marks.given: the three known numbers, the three blanks and the median are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers five, twenty one and fourteen, three blanks, and a median of thirteen.
beats.on_screen: Given: 5, 21, 14 and three blanks; median = 13

marks.find: the words fills for the blanks and how many are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to fill the blanks and say how many fills there can be.
beats.on_screen: To find: fills for the blanks, and how many there are

marks.pair: the 3rd and 4th, 12 and 14, are circled with 12 + 14 = 26
marks.sort: the six numbers slide into sorted order

narration: <bookmark mark='fill'/>Step one, try one, twelve and fourteen in the blanks.
<bookmark mark='sort'/>Sorted, the list is one, five, twelve, fourteen, fourteen, twenty one.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>The third and fourth values are twelve and fourteen.
They add to twenty six, so the median is thirteen.

marks.pair: the 3rd and 4th, 13 and 13, are circled with 13 + 13 = 26

narration: <bookmark mark='fill'/>Step two, try twelve, thirteen and thirteen.
The sorted list is five, twelve, thirteen, thirteen, fourteen, twenty one.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>The third and fourth values are thirteen and thirteen, which add to twenty six.
This fill works too.

marks.grow: the third blank n takes the values 14, 15, 16 and keeps growing
marks.keep: 3 and 12 stay fixed in two blanks
marks.pair: the 3rd and 4th stay 12 and 14 each time

narration: <bookmark mark='keep'/>Step three, keep three and twelve in two blanks.
Let the third blank be any number from fourteen upwards.
<bookmark mark='grow'/>Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, and the numbers never stop.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>Each time, the third and fourth sorted values stay twelve and fourteen.
Every one of these fills works.
beats.on_screen: blanks 3, 12 and n, with n = 14, 15, 16, ...: the 3rd and 4th stay 12 and 14

marks.pair: the 3rd and 4th, 12 and 14, are circled with the median 13

narration: <bookmark mark='fill'/>Check one big case, with three, twelve and one hundred.
The sorted list is three, five, twelve, fourteen, twenty one, one hundred.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>Twelve and fourteen add to twenty six, so the median is thirteen.

marks.ans: the answer is boxed beside the example

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>There are infinitely many possibilities, for example one, twelve and fourteen.
beats.on_screen: Answer: infinitely many possibilities, for example 1, 12, 14

final_answer.value: infinitely many
final_answer.spoken: there are infinitely many possibilities

media.title: How many ways can two blanks give a mean of six point five?
media.context: Tales by Dots and Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two blanks sit among the numbers three, eleven, fifteen and six, and the mean of all six must be six point five. The mean gives the total, the known numbers leave four for the blanks, and counting numbers give only a few pairs.

video_script.why: A child who has found one missing value from a mean now finds how many pairs of missing values fit.

marks.ask: the words how many fills appear with an empty box
marks.row: the row of six boxes appears with two blanks
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Six boxes hold three, eleven, two blanks, fifteen and six.
<bookmark mark='mean'/>Fill the blanks so that the mean of all six numbers is six point five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many fills are there if only counting numbers are allowed?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a row of six boxes holding 3, 11, a blank, a blank, 15, 6; the words mean 6.5

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

<bookmark mark='rest'/>The two blanks must make up whatever the known numbers leave out.

marks.given: the four known numbers, the two blanks and the mean are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers three, eleven, fifteen and six, two blanks, and a mean of six point five.

marks.find: the words the fills and how many are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to fill the two blanks and count the fills.
beats.on_screen: To find: the fills for the two blanks, and how many there are

narration: <bookmark mark='times'/>Step one, turn the mean into the total.
Multiply six point five by six.
<bookmark mark='total'/>The total of all six numbers is thirty nine.

marks.add: the four known numbers are added one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step two, add the four known numbers.
Three, eleven, fifteen and six.

marks.left: the two blanks must add to 4

<bookmark mark='left'/>The two blanks must add up to four.

marks.same: 3 and 1 is joined to 1 and 3 as the same collection
marks.count: counting numbers 1, 2, 3 are listed and zero is crossed out
marks.pairs: the pairs 1 and 3, and 2 and 2, are written

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step four, list the pairs of counting numbers that add to four.
Counting numbers start at one, so zero is not allowed.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>One and three add to four, and so do two and two.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Three and one is the same collection as one and three.
The order does not change the mean.
beats.on_screen: counting numbers start at 1: 1 + 3 = 4 and 2 + 2 = 4; 3 + 1 is the same collection as 1 + 3; 0 + 4 is not allowed

marks.one: 1 and 3 go into the blanks and 39 ÷ 6 = 6.5 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Check both fills.
With one and three, the total is thirty nine.
Thirty nine divided by six is six point five.
<bookmark mark='two'/>With two and two, the total is thirty nine again, so the mean is six point five.

media.title: Frequency Table Lab
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, The Balancing Act: Mean and Median). Change the frequencies and watch the total, mean and median change. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student opens a table of the family sizes of a class of 36 students. The value column runs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, and the frequency column reads 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1 and 1, with every frequency editable. Beside them are a value times frequency column, a running total column, a Total and Count row, and read-outs for the mean and the median. Under the table a dot plot of stacked dots is redrawn the moment a frequency changes.

First the student predicts. The sizes run from 3 to 10, and 4 occurs 11 times while 10 occurs once, so will the true average be bigger or smaller than 6.5, the middle of the two ends? Then the student fills the value times frequency column: 9, 44, 45, 42, 21, 8, 9 and 10. The total is 188 over a count of 36, so the mean is about 5.22, and the balance point of the dot plot sits there, below 6.5. For the median the student first says that with 36 values it lies between the 18th and 19th. The running total column reads 3, 14, 23 and on up to 36, and the row for size 5 is highlighted because it holds positions 15 to 23. Both middle values are 5, so the median is 5 and not a single value had to be written out.

The six cards are the mean (about 5.22), the median (5), a change of one frequency with a prediction, a table of the student's own with mean equal to median, the shortcut check, and a table with a median of 3. For the third card the student raises the frequency of size 10 from 1 to 2, predicts that the mean rises, and sees it move to about 5.35. For the fourth the student can try a table that is the same on both sides of its middle value. For the fifth the lab shows the tempting shortcuts beside 5.22: adding the eight sizes once each and dividing by 8 gives 6.5, and adding the frequencies and dividing by 8 gives 4.5. A frequency average earns a warning with the value times frequency steps shown. For the last the student chooses values and frequencies until the running total passes the middle position at the value 3.

Hints go in order: what does each frequency say about how many times a value appears? Then: multiply each value by its frequency before adding. Then: the total of value times frequency, divided by the total frequency, is the mean. Last, the steps are shown, the median row is highlighted and a new table follows. Through doing, the student learns that each value counts as often as it occurs, and that the median is found where the running total passes the middle position.

tool_config.idea: With a frequency table the total is the sum of value times frequency, and the median is found by running totals of the frequencies, not by averaging the raw frequencies.

media.description: A table lists family sizes from three to ten and how many students have each size. Each size is multiplied by its frequency, the amounts are added, and the total is divided by thirty six students. Keeko doubts this and divides the frequencies by the eight sizes.

video_script.why: A child who finds a mean from a short list meets a frequency table for the first time.

marks.ask: the words mean family size appear with an empty box
marks.book: the title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean.
<bookmark mark='story'/>The teacher asks every student how many people live in the family.
<bookmark mark='table'/>The answers go into a table.
The top row shows the number of people in a family, from three to ten.
The bottom row shows how many students have each number.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the mean number of people in a family of the class?
beats.on_screen: title card From your book; the teacher at the board; a table with family values 3 to 10 in the top row and student counts 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1 in the bottom row Photo: A classroom with rows of benches

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the table and the question stay on the board

marks.big: size 4 is shown 11 times in a row of small dots, size 3 only 3 times
marks.freq: the bottom row is labelled frequency

narration: <bookmark mark='freq'/>The number of students for each family value is called the frequency.
<bookmark mark='big'/>A value with a big frequency occurs many times in the data.
The value four occurs eleven times, and the value three only three times.
beats.on_screen: the bottom row labelled frequency; size 3 has frequency 3, size 4 has frequency 11

marks.given: the sizes and their frequencies are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, family values from three to ten.
Their frequencies are three, eleven, nine, seven, three, one, one and one.

marks.find: the words the mean family size are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the mean number of people in a family of the class.
beats.on_screen: To find: the mean family size

marks.add: the eight frequencies are added one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step one, add the frequencies to count the students.
Three plus eleven plus nine plus seven plus three plus one plus one plus one.
<bookmark mark='total'/>That gives thirty six students.

marks.p3: 7 × 3 = 21 is written, then 8, 9 and 10 each written with × 1

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, multiply each family value by its frequency, because a common value counts more.
<bookmark mark='p1'/>Three times three is nine.
Four times eleven is forty four.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>Five times nine is forty five.
Six times seven is forty two.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>Seven times three is twenty one.
The values eight, nine and ten occur once each, so they give eight, nine and ten.

marks.add: the eight amounts line up in a row
marks.rest: 21, 8, 9 and 10 are added on to reach 188

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step three, add the amounts to get the total of all the family members.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Nine plus forty four plus forty five plus forty two is one hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Adding twenty one, eight, nine and ten gives one hundred and eighty eight.

marks.rule: the line mean = total ÷ students appears

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step four, the mean is the total divided by the number of students.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Divide one hundred and eighty eight by thirty six.
beats.on_screen: mean = total ÷ students = 188 ÷ 36

marks.ans: the answer is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The mean number of people in a family is about five point two two.
beats.on_screen: Answer: mean ≈ 5.22

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
<bookmark mark='use'/>A shopkeeper wants the mean number of people in a family near his shop.
He counts how many families have each number of people.
Then he multiplies, adds and divides, so big groups count for more.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question: What is the real-life use case? The figure shows the real use named in the narration. Photo: Sacks of rice in a ration shop

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
<bookmark mark='slip'/>Some students think the mean is four point five.
They add the frequencies to get thirty six and divide by the eight values.
But thirty six counts students, not family members, so the values never entered the sum.
Each value must be multiplied by its frequency, because a value shared by many students counts for more.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question: What mistake do some students make here? The figure shows the wrong idea crossed out and the right working beside it.

<bookmark mark='dot'/>Each dot is one student.
<bookmark mark='twice'/>Four students rode their cycles twice.

<bookmark mark='first'/>That gives zero, one, eight, twenty one and twenty eight.

The first says everyone cycled at least once.

<bookmark mark='b'/>The second says almost everyone cycled a few times.

<bookmark mark='c'/>The third says some students cycled twice on a day.
<bookmark mark='c2'/>A week has seven days, so eight or ten rides need a day with two rides.
It is valid.

content.text:
What is the average family size of students in your class? How would you find this out?
We can collect the data of how many family members each student has, add them up, and divide it by the number of students. The family size data of students in a class is shown in the table.
Some of you may have thought, Easy! (3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10) ÷ 8 = 52 ÷ 8 = 6.5.
Remember that finding the average involves adding all the values in the data. The number 3 occurs three times, the number 4 occurs eleven times, and so on. Do these reflect in your calculation?
Accounting for the frequencies of each value, the average is 188 ÷ 36 = 5.22. The average family size of this class is 5.22.

concepts.concept_name: The mean of a frequency table

content.text:
What is the median family size of this class? We know that there are 36 values in the data. The median would be the average of the 18th and 19th value in the sequence when the data is ordered.
Do we need to write all the 36 numbers in order? Is there a quicker way to find out? We can make use of the table where the frequencies are listed.
Adding the frequencies of 3 and 4, we get 3 + 11 = 14. This means the value in the 14th position when the data is sorted is 4. Adding the frequencies of 3, 4, and 5, we get 3 + 11 + 9 = 23. We can see that all the values from positions 15 to 23 are 5. Therefore, the median of this data is 5.

media.title: Spreadsheet Simulator
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, The Balancing Act: Mean and Median). Rows, columns and cells. Build SUM and AVERAGE formulas! Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student sees a small spreadsheet of Sudhakar's class marks. Column letters A to H run across the top and row numbers down the side. Row 1 holds the headings Name, Odia, Telugu, English, Maths, Social, Science and Total, and rows 2 to 8 hold Ratna, Nagesh, Ashwin, Farooq, Mrinal, Gowri and Pankaj with six marks each. Above the grid are a name box that shows the cell under the pointer and a formula bar, and beside it are two buttons, SUM and AVERAGE, that start a formula over a selected range.

The student begins by finding cells. Before clicking, the student predicts where Farooq's Maths mark sits by counting the column letter and the row number, then clicks it. The name box reads E5 and the formula bar shows 42. Next the student drags across a run of cells. The selection glows and its name appears as Start:End. Across Nagesh's row it reads B3:G3 and the tool counts 6 cells, and down the English column for the first five students it reads D2:D6.

Then comes the typing. In H3 the student types =SUM(B3:G3), and the result 250 is checked against the marks added by hand: 41, 43, 48, 39, 40 and 39. For Gowri, who scored 27, 29 and 34 in Odia, Telugu and English, the student first guesses whether the average is above or below 30, then types =AVERAGE(B7:D7) and sees that the three cells are added and divided by 3, giving 30. A wrong range shows the cells it really used and their values: B7:C7 uses only 27 and 29 and gives 28, and B3:F3 leaves out G3 and gives 211 instead of 250. On the next card the student changes one cell, for example Gowri's Odia mark from 27 to 30, predicts the new sum and average, and watches every formula that includes the cell update, here from 90 to 93 and from 30 to 31. On the last card the student types =AVERAGE over a whole subject column, such as B2:B8 for Odia, and compares it with the Telugu column to see which subject has the higher average.

Hints go in order: which letter and number name the cell you want? Then: a range joins two corner cells with a colon. Then: SUM over the range adds the values, and AVERAGE divides that sum by the number of cells. Last, the range is highlighted, the sum and average are shown and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a cell is named by its column and row, that Start:End names a run of cells, and that SUM and AVERAGE do in one step what adding and dividing do by hand.

content.text:
Sudhakar has collected the mid-term exam marks obtained by his Grade 8 students in a table of 22 students and 6 subjects.
Sudhakar has to calculate the total marks scored by each student. He is also interested in knowing the average marks scored in each subject. But there are so many numbers! Is there any way to further quicken this process?
A spreadsheet is like a digital notebook with rows and columns of small boxes called cells. In each cell, we can type text or numbers.
Can you tell which cell has the marks obtained by Farooq in Mathematics? Cells are named by the column headers A, B, C, … and row headers 1, 2, 3, … Farooq's score in Mathematics is in cell E5.
Can you tell what data is in column B7? In which subjects has Ashwin scored more than 30 marks?
We can describe a row of cells by an expression of the form Start:End. Nagesh's marks are described by B3:G3, Gowri's marks in Odia, Telugu and English by B7:D7, and D2:D6 describes the marks in English for the first five students.

content.text:
We can also enter formulae in a cell. We can write a formula that computes the sum or average of a row, or column of cells.
=SUM(B3:G3) calculates the total marks for Nagesh across all subjects, while =AVERAGE(B7:D7) calculates Gowri's average marks across Odia, Telugu and English.
What formula would you type to find out the class average marks in Science? Find out if the class average marks in Odia is greater than the class average marks in Telugu. Show the average marks in other subjects after the last row by typing the appropriate formulae. Get the total scores of each student by typing the appropriate formulae.
Note to the teacher: any spreadsheet application can be used, and students can share a computer in groups, or the screen can be projected.

Worked example: Nagesh's marks are 41, 43, 48, 39, 40 and 39. Find his total, and say the formula.
1. Add: 41 + 43 = 84, 84 + 48 = 132, 132 + 39 = 171, 171 + 40 = 211, 211 + 39 = 250.
2. The formula over his row is =SUM(B3:G3).
Answer: His total is 250, found with =SUM(B3:G3)

media.title: Line Graph Builder
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, Visualising and Interpreting Data). Pick a scale, plot dots, join them, read the line. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student faces a blank grid with a data table beside it. The axis names and the scale are boxes for the student to fill: what goes along the bottom, what goes up the side, where the scale starts, its top value and its step. Below the grid are a Plot button, a Join button and a switch that adds a second series with its own mark and colour.

Card 1 is a shop's week. Customers visiting from Monday to Sunday are 16, 19, 10, 14, 20, 22 and 35. The student writes days along the bottom and number of customers up the side, then chooses a scale. A top value of 40 in steps of 5 fits the largest value, 35. Each table row is dragged onto the grid, with time across and the value up, and the points are then joined in the order of the days. A point dropped in the wrong spot shows the table value it should match. Card 2 adds the customers who purchased, 10, 8, 7, 11, 12, 16 and 26, as a second line with a different mark and colour and a key. The student sees that both lines rise towards the weekend and that purchasing stays below visiting every day.

Card 3 plots Punjab's monthly highest temperature, which runs from about 19 degrees in January up to 38 in June, just under 35 in July and about 23 in December. Card 4 is a deliberate mistake. The student sets the top of the scale to 30 and the hot months, such as June at 38, appear as markers that do not fit, so the student sees why the scale must be chosen to fit the biggest value. Card 5 gives the price of iodised salt each January from 2016 to 2025 for six states. The student picks three, for example Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, chooses a scale from 0 to 30 and plots each as its own line. Card 6 asks which line rises most and why a line graph suits the data. West Bengal rises most, from 9.47 to 23.99, about 14.52 rupees, and a line graph shows how a value changes from one year to the next. After each finished graph the tool asks for a one-line summary of the trend.

Hints go in order: what goes along the bottom and what goes up the side? Then: pick the scale so the biggest value fits and the points are not squeezed. Then: each row of the table is one point, with time across and value up. Last, the points are placed and joined in order, the trend is described and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns the four moves of a line graph, which are to label the axes, pick the scale, plot each point and join them in order, and that two lines on one grid need different marks or colours and a key.

content.text:
5.2 Visualising and Interpreting Data
So far we have learnt how to read and make pictographs, bar graphs, clustered-bar graphs, and dot plots. We now examine some more ways of visualising data.
The following figure is a clustered-column graph that shows the monthly maximum temperature in Kerala and Punjab in 2023. Now, observe the following graph. Do both these graphs represent the same information?
We call such a graph made up of lines a line graph. Line graphs are generally used to visualise data across time.
How do we get the maximum temperature over a month in a state? There could be a few weather stations across the state that regularly track the local temperature. We can get the monthly maximum temperature by looking at the maximum value among all the values recorded across the state.

content.text:
Worked example: Kerala's April column reaches about 33 degrees and its July column about 29 degrees. Where do these two months sit on the line graph, and what does the line between them show?
1. Each month's point sits at the top of its column: April at about 33, July at about 29.
2. The line joins the points in month order, so from April to July it slopes down.
3. The drop is about 33 − 29 = 4 degrees.
Answer: April's point is at about 33 and July's at about 29; the line slopes down by about 4 degrees

content.text:
To identify and interpret the information presented, let us follow a two-step process.
Step 1: Identify what is given. Notice how the graph is organised, what scale is used, and what patterns the data shows. The data for each month for a city is marked and connected by lines to show the change over time. Kerala's data is shown using blue circle marks connected by blue lines and Punjab's data is shown in red. The horizontal line shows the months of the year. The vertical line shows the temperature in degrees Celsius.
The different shape markers help in easily distinguishing if the graph is printed in greyscale, or for people who find it difficult to distinguish colour.
Step 2: Infer and interpret from what is given. In Punjab, the monthly maximum temperature increases from January to June, reaching a high of 38 degrees. Then, it reduces to just under 35 degrees in July, stays mostly flat till September, and then falls continuously till December, reaching about 23 degrees. January has the lowest, about 19 degrees.
Kerala's trend is different: it stays mostly flat throughout the year. The peak is around 33 degrees in April and the lowest point is around 29 degrees in July. In short, the temperature in Punjab varies more, reaching colder and warmer temperatures than in Kerala.

content.text:
This can trigger questions in different directions, some of which can be answered using data. Here are some directions to think about:

content.text:
Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 9): A table gives the retail price in rupees of iodised salt in January over 10 years, 2016 to 2025, for Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam, Gujarat, Mizoram, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. (i) Show any 3 states as a line graph with a suitable scale. (ii) What do you find interesting? (iii) Compare the price variation in Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh. (iv) In which state did the price rise the most from 2016 to 2025? (v) What are you curious to explore further?
1. (i) Years 2016 to 2025 along the bottom; prices from 0 to 30 rupees up the side in steps of 5, with one line per state.
2. (iii) Gujarat stays near 14 to 15 rupees for most years and jumps to 19.2 only in 2025. Uttar Pradesh climbs steadily from 16.15 to 26.9 and then dips to 24.81, so it varies much more.
3. (iv) Rise from 2016 to 2025: Andaman and Nicobar Islands 20.99 − 16 = 4.99, Assam 12.35 − 6 = 6.35, Gujarat 19.2 − 16.5 = 2.7, Mizoram 29.8 − 20 = 9.8, Uttar Pradesh 24.81 − 16.15 = 8.66, West Bengal 23.99 − 9.47 = 14.52. The biggest rise is in West Bengal.
4. (ii) and (v) are open: for example, why West Bengal's price rose from 9.47 to 23.99, and whether the same happens with other food items.
Answer: West Bengal rose the most, by about 14.52 rupees; Gujarat varied less than Uttar Pradesh
