media.title: Graph Interpreter
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, Visualising and Interpreting Data). Read real graphs, tap the points and test each claim. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A busy line graph fills the screen. The years 2012 to 2024 run along the bottom, the number of objects launched into space runs up the side to 3000, and four lines labelled World, United States, China and Russia each carry a different mark. Beside the graph are a steepness ruler and a statement panel in which every statement gets a Valid or Not valid switch.

The student works in two steps. Step 1 asks what is given, the axes, the scale and what each line stands for, before any reading is allowed. Step 2 asks what the graph says. Tapping a point shows its place on the graph, and the student reads the value off the scale. Card 1 asks for the World count in 2023, and an answer near 2900 is accepted as about 2900. Card 2 compares the United States rise from 2022 to 2023 with the rise from 2023 to 2024. The student lays the ruler along each segment and sees about 280 against about 30, so the steeper segment is the bigger change. Card 3 asks for two consecutive years in which the World count at least doubled. Sliding the ruler along, the student finds 2016 to 2017, about 230 to 480, and 2019 to 2020, about 600 to 1270.

Card 4 shows four statements to mark. The World count rose every year is not valid, because the line falls in 2018 and in 2024. The United States launched about three fourths of the World count in 2022 to 2024 is valid, about 2250 out of 2850. Nepal launched nothing in 2012 to 2024 is not valid, because Nepal is not on the graph and a missing line says nothing. China and Russia together made about 400 in 2024 is valid, about 280 plus 120. A wrong mark highlights the part of the graph that supports or breaks the statement. Card 5 asks why the three countries do not make up the World line. In 2024 they add to about 2650 against about 2850, so about 200 objects come from countries that are not shown. Card 6 opens a second graph of the main source of lighting in rural and urban homes. The student again names the axes and the lines, then marks statements. A statement is valid only if the lines support it, so one about power cuts is not, since no line shows power cuts. Each graph ends with one summary sentence from the student.

Hints go in order: what are the axes and what does each line stand for? Then: find the value on the line and read across to the scale. Then: compare how steep the two segments are, since the steeper one is the bigger change. Last, the reading and the steepness are shown, the statement is judged and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns to read the axes and the scale first and the shape second, and that a statement is valid only when the graph supports it.

content.text:
Space Jam: A Traffic Problem in the Future? Take a look at the line graph showing the annual number of objects launched into space. What could be the possible method used to derive this data? Discuss.
Step 1: Identify what is given. Notice how the graph is organised, what scale is used, and what patterns the data shows.
Step 2: Infer from and interpret what is given. In 2024, the worldwide count is around 2800, whereas in 2023, it was around 2900. We can say that 2023 saw the highest number of objects launched into space worldwide, assuming the trend before 2012 was decreasing.
The counts of the three countries don't add up to the worldwide count. Therefore, we can infer that the counts of other countries are not shown in this visualisation.

content.text:
Worked example: In 2024 the World line is about 2850, the United States about 2250, China about 280 and Russia about 120. Do the three countries make up the World count?
1. Add the three countries: 2250 + 280 + 120 = 2650.
2. Compare with the World: 2850 − 2650 = 200.
3. About 200 objects came from countries the graph does not show.
Answer: No; about 200 objects come from other countries that are not shown

For the USA, the increase from 2022 to 2023 is more than from 2023 to 2024. We can say this by looking at how steep the line segments are: the steeper the line is, the greater the increase.
Which of the following statements are valid inferences? From 2012 till 2024, the worldwide count of space object launches increased every year. USA is a major contributor in the years 2022 to 24, launching about three fourths of the worldwide count. Nepal did not launch any object in the period 2012 to 24. The combined count of object launches by China and Russia in 2024 is about 400.
Identify two consecutive years where the worldwide count increased by 2 times or more.

4. A doubling: 2016 to 2017 goes from about 230 to 480, and 2019 to 2020 goes from about 600 to 1270.

concepts.concept_name: Steeper means a bigger change

content.text:
Imagine the same data being shown as a clustered column graph. There would be 13 clusters, one for each year, and within each cluster, 4 columns, making a total of 52 bars! Such a graph would look crowded and difficult to read, making it hard to interpret the trends clearly.
A line graph, on the other hand, is better suited for illustrating changes over time. By connecting data points with line segments, it provides a clear visual representation of trends and variations, allowing the reader to easily track how a parameter evolves across different years.

Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 10): Referring to the graph of the primary source of lighting in rural and urban homes, which statements are valid and why? (i) In 1983 most rural homes used kerosene and most urban homes electricity. (ii) Kerosene use has decreased over time in both rural and urban areas. (iii) In the year 2000, 10% of urban households used electricity. (iv) In 2023 there were no power cuts.
1. Read the two lines for kerosene and two for electricity, for rural and urban, in each year.
2. (i) Valid if the rural kerosene line is above half in 1983 and the urban electricity line is above half.
3. (ii) Valid if both kerosene lines slope down over the years.
4. (iii) Check the urban electricity line at 2000. It is far higher than 10%, so this is not valid.
5. (iv) The graph shows the main source of lighting, not power cuts, so it cannot support this.
Answer: Check (i) and (ii) against the lines; (iii) is not valid; (iv) is not supported by the graph

Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 11): A line graph shows the average daily time rural and urban kids spend on hobbies and games by age. (i) How long do children aged 10 in urban areas spend each day? (ii) At what age do rural kids spend 1.5 hours? Choose from 8, 10, 12, 14 and 18 years. (iii) Are these correct? (a) The average time at age 15 is twice that at age 10. (b) All rural kids aged 15 spend at least 1 hour a day.
1. (i) Find age 10 on the bottom axis, go up to the urban line and read across.
2. (ii) Find 1.5 hours on the side scale, go across to the rural line and read the age below it.
3. (iii) (a) Divide the age 15 value by the age 10 value and see if it is about 2. (b) The graph gives an average, so it says nothing about every child: not correct.
Answer: Read from the graph; (b) cannot be concluded because it is an average

media.title: Rain Map Compare
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, Visualising and Interpreting Data). Compare the rainy days of four cities, month by month. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A map of India fills the left side of the screen, with six city pins waiting beside it: Kovalam, Udupi, Mumbai, Rameswaram, Chennai and Puri. On the right is a line graph of monthly average rainfall from January to December, on which any city's line can be switched on or off, and under it a grouping panel.

The student drags each pin to the city's place on the map. A pin dropped in the wrong place returns to the map with its coast named. A placed city brings its line onto the graph, and all lines share one scale, so the student must compare them on the same scale before saying that one city gets more rain. Card 1 uses the three west coast cities. The student switches their lines on, drops a peak marker on the highest point of each and reads the month underneath. All three peak in June to August, and Udupi reaches about 880 millimetres in July. Tapping a point reminds the student that the value is an average of that month over several years, so four Junes of 820, 900, 760 and 920 millimetres give 850, a typical June and not a real one.

Card 2 does the same for the east coast. Rameswaram gets most of its rain in October to December and very little from January to September, Chennai starts getting rain from June and peaks in November, and Puri peaks in July to September. A wrong peak month shows the highest point of that city's line. Card 3 asks which city has the highest peak, and the answer is Udupi. Card 4 asks the student to place low-point markers and find the dry months common to all six, which are January to March. Card 5 asks the student to drag the cities into groups by peak season: June to August, July to September and October to December. The grouping is checked against the peak seasons. Card 6 asks why Puri differs from the other east coast cities. It lies on the east coast but peaks in July to September, within the months of the south west monsoon, while Rameswaram and Chennai peak in the months of the north east monsoon. So the coast alone does not decide the month, the winds do.

Hints go in order: which cities lie on the west coast and which on the east coast? Then: look for the highest point on each line and read the month below it. Then: compare peak months across the six lines on one scale. Last, the peak months are shown on the map and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns to read peaks and dry months off a line graph, and to link when a place gets its rain with its coast and its monsoon.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how would you get one number for June in Udupi when every year's June is different?
2. Collect the June rainfall of several years. Add them and divide by the number of years.
3. Do the same for every month. The line is then the typical year, not any one real year.

content.text:
Worked example: Suppose a town's June rainfall over 4 years was 820, 900, 760 and 920 millimetres. What is its monthly average rainfall for June?
1. Add the four Junes: 820 + 900 + 760 + 920 = 3400.
2. Divide by the number of years: 3400 ÷ 4 = 850.
Answer: 850 millimetres, the typical June, not any one real June

Worked example: Mumbai's rain peaks in July and Chennai's in November. Which monsoon brings each peak?

2. The north east monsoon reaches the south east coast in October to December, which covers November.
3. So Mumbai's peak comes from the south west monsoon and Chennai's from the north east monsoon.

(i) At which place does the sun rise earliest in January, and about how long is the day there? (ii) Which place has the longest day over the year? (iii) What do you find interesting?
1. Sunrise is the lower line in the morning and sunset the upper line in the evening, since sunrise is earlier in the day.
2. (i) Find the lowest sunrise value in January across the four places. Day length is sunset minus sunrise, about 10 to 11 hours.
3. (ii) The place where the gap between the sunset and sunrise lines is widest over the year.
4. (iii) Each line repeats a smooth up and down pattern every year.
Answer: Read the values from the graph and give them as approximate

content.text:
Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 15): A graph shows moonrise and moonset times over a month. (i) On what dates were amavasya (new moon) and purnima (full moon)? (ii) What do you notice? What do you wonder?
1. On new moon day the moon rises and sets about with the sun, so moonrise is in the morning and moonset in the evening.
2. On full moon day the moon rises about when the sun sets, so moonrise is in the evening and moonset in the morning.
3. Look for those dates on the graph. Each moon time shifts about 50 minutes later every day.
4. (ii) is open: for example, why the moon is not in the sky at the same time every day.
Answer: Dates are read from the graph where moonrise is near sunrise (new moon) and near sunset (full moon)

media.title: Infographic Map: Rice and Wheat
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12), Infographics: rice or wheat? Per-person rice minus wheat preference by state, 68th NSS 2011-12, boundaries as in 2011.
media.description:
A tall map of India with every state coloured fills the screen, and beside it runs a colour bar from minus 100 at the wheat end to plus 100 at the rice end. On the right are a ranking list, a threshold slider and a note box. One state, Karnataka, is shown grey with a question mark. A switch can draw the red line that splits the rice states from the wheat states.

The student taps states to read them. A tap shows the state's name, its value and its colour marked on the bar. Card 1 asks for Punjab, about minus 78, and what that says: Punjab strongly prefers wheat. Bihar, close to 0, is about balanced. On the cards that follow, the student taps and ranks the top five rice states and the top five wheat states. The rice list is Manipur about plus 100, Nagaland plus 99, Mizoram plus 97, Tripura plus 96 and Meghalaya plus 95. The wheat list is Rajasthan about minus 93, Haryana minus 81, Punjab minus 78, Madhya Pradesh minus 60 and Delhi minus 45. A wrong ranking shows the true order with the values.

Next the student drags the threshold slider outwards from 0. States whose value lies inside the band light up, and with a band of minus 20 to plus 20 states such as Bihar and Maharashtra, at about minus 15, are among them. The student names a few balanced states from what lights up. For Karnataka the student first guesses rice or wheat, then reads the neighbours' values: Goa plus 57, Kerala plus 79, Tamil Nadu plus 85, Andhra Pradesh plus 92 and Maharashtra minus 15. Four of the five lean to rice, so the student places a guess on the bar. A guess in the rice leaning range of roughly plus 60 to plus 80 is accepted as reasoned, a guess that ignores the neighbours is questioned, and the tool says that a value found this way is an estimate, not a fact. The last card asks what plus 100 means. A claim that it means only rice is eaten is corrected with the scale text: it means that the gap between rice and wheat eating is the largest, not that no wheat is eaten.

Hints go in order: what does the colour of a state stand for? Then: use the scale at the top to turn the colour into a number. Then: positive is rice, negative is wheat, and near zero is balanced. Last, the value is shown with its meaning and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns to read a colour scale as a number line, to rank and compare values on a map, and to estimate a hidden value from its neighbours.

content.text:
Infographics. In Grade 6, we saw an example of how infographics can be used to communicate information and insights more clearly and quickly in a visually appealing way. Take a look at the following infographic. Are you able to understand the information presented here?
This infographic compares the preference between rice and wheat in different states. The colour scale at the top right indicates how to interpret the different shades in terms of preferences.
The difference between the per capita consumption of rice and wheat is mapped to values between −100 and +100. A value of +100 doesn't mean that the state doesn't consume wheat at all. It means that this state prefers mostly rice and the difference between per capita rice and wheat consumption is the highest.
Isn't it interesting how there is a clear geographical split in preferences of rice vs. wheat shown by the red line?

content.text:
1. Predict first: on a map of India, where would you expect people to prefer rice, and where wheat?
2. Each state has one number between −100 and +100. A positive number means rice is preferred, a negative number means wheat is preferred, near zero means about equal.
3. +100 does not mean no wheat is eaten. It means the gap between rice and wheat is the largest possible.
4. The red line on the map splits the rice states from the wheat states.

content.text:
Worked example: On the scale, Punjab is −78 and Bihar is close to 0. What does each value say about rice and wheat?
1. A negative value means wheat is preferred, so Punjab leans strongly to wheat.
2. Punjab is 78 steps from 0, close to the wheat end at −100.
3. A value near 0 means the two are eaten in about equal amounts, so Bihar is balanced.
Answer: Punjab strongly prefers wheat; Bihar is about balanced

content.text:
1. Predict first: Karnataka's value is hidden. Its neighbours are Goa, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. Before looking at the neighbours, would you guess rice or wheat?
2. Top rice states read from the map are Manipur about +100, Nagaland +99, Mizoram +97, Tripura +96 and Meghalaya +95. Top wheat states are Rajasthan about −93, Haryana −81, Punjab −78, Madhya Pradesh −60 and Delhi −45.
3. States near zero, such as Bihar, are balanced.
4. Karnataka's neighbours Goa +57, Kerala +79, Tamil Nadu +85 and Andhra Pradesh +92 lean to rice, while Maharashtra is −15. A reasonable guess is a rice leaning value, roughly +60 to +80.

content.text:
Worked example: Use the neighbours' values to guess Karnataka's value: Goa +57, Kerala +79, Tamil Nadu +85, Andhra Pradesh +92, Maharashtra −15.
1. Four of the five neighbours are strongly rice.
2. Maharashtra is slightly towards wheat.
3. The average of the five is (57 + 79 + 85 + 92 − 15) ÷ 5 = 298 ÷ 5 = 59.6.
4. Karnataka is probably a little above or around this, so about +60 to +80.
Answer: A rice leaning value of about +60 to +80, an estimate

content.text:
Worked example: Manipur is about +100 and Rajasthan about −93. How far apart are they on the scale, and what data could explain the gap?
1. The distance is 100 − (−93) = 193 steps on the scale.
2. That is almost the whole scale of 200 steps.
3. Rainfall data for the two states could help explain it, since rice needs much more water.
Answer: 193 steps apart; rainfall data could help explain the gap

media.title: Activity Strip Painter
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, Visualising and Interpreting Data). Paint a day on a 48-box strip, then read what strips say! Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A long strip of 48 empty boxes runs across the screen from midnight to midnight. Each box is numbered and stands for 30 minutes, and the strip is marked at midnight and noon. Under it are a colour key of activities such as sleeping, eating, school, studying, travelling, friends and media, a paint brush, and a read-out of the hours spent on each activity. A second strip below the first is used for comparing.

The student picks a colour and drags the brush across boxes to paint. As the brush moves, the box under it shows its start time, since box n starts (n minus 1) times 30 minutes after midnight, and the read-out counts the painted boxes and turns them into hours at two boxes to an hour. Card 1 asks for 8 hours of sleep, which takes 16 boxes. Card 2 asks the student to paint a school day from 9:30 am to 4:30 pm, which runs from box 20 to box 33 and covers 14 boxes, or 7 hours. A wrong box count shows the boxes selected and the hours they make. A day painted as 18 boxes of sleep, 14 of school and 16 of other things reads 9, 7 and 8 hours, which add up to the 24 hours of a day.

Card 3 reverses the task. The student is given box 19 and has to find when it starts. After 18 boxes, which is 9 hours, it begins at 9:00 am. Card 4 asks the student to paint their own weekday on the top strip and a holiday on the second strip. If sleep is 8 hours on a weekday and 10 on a holiday, that is 16 boxes against 20, which is 4 more boxes, or 2 more hours. The comparison highlights the boxes that differ. Card 5 compares the student's strip with an adult's. Card 6 shows a ready-made strip, and the student finds the longest block and names the activity from the key. The student can guess the day too: a long block of class colour with travel on either side suggests a school day, and a long unbroken block of friends and media suggests the day of a long movie. One colour used for two activities is flagged against the key, since the same colour must always mean the same activity.

Hints go in order: how many boxes make one hour? Then: two boxes are an hour, so count the boxes and divide by two. Then: the boxes from the start of the block to the end give the hours. Last, the boxes are counted, the hours are shown and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a whole day can be held on 48 boxes, that counting boxes gives time, and that two strips painted in one key can be compared box by box.

topics.summary: A strip stores a whole day in 48 boxes of 30 minutes each; a line graph with many close points looks smooth, and zooming in shows detail.

content.text:
What can a Strip Say? Manoj has an interesting hobby. He makes note of what he does throughout the day. He records his activities by colouring a strip of paper with 48 boxes, marking time in 30 minute intervals from midnight to midnight.
He has recorded five types of activities for three different days of the week on three coloured strips: sleeping, eating, meeting friends, hobbies, media, time with family, attending classes, studying and homework, showering and getting dressed, yoga or exercise, and travelling.
Look at the three coloured strips carefully. What activity does each colour stand for?
The three strips correspond to the days Friday to Sunday in some order. Which day do you think each strip represents?
On one of these days, he went out with friends to watch a long movie. When do you think this happened?
At what time does his school break for lunch? What more can the strips tell us?

content.text:
1. Predict first: 48 boxes of 30 minutes cover a whole day. How many boxes make one hour, and what time does box 19 start?
2. 2 boxes make an hour, so 48 boxes make 24 hours. Box 19 starts after 18 boxes, which is 9 hours after midnight, at 9:00 am.
3. Use the key to see which colour is which activity. A strip with a long block of the class colour and a travel colour before and after is a school day, and the strip with a long unbroken block of the friends and media colour is the movie day.
4. Compare the three strips: when he wakes up, how long he sleeps, how much time goes to meals.

content.text:
Worked example: Manoj's school runs from 9:30 am to 4:30 pm. How many boxes of his strip does the school block cover, and which box does it start at?
1. From 9:30 am to 4:30 pm is 7 hours.
2. Each hour is 2 boxes, so the block is 7 × 2 = 14 boxes.
3. 9:30 am is 9 hours 30 minutes after midnight, which is 19 boxes, so the block starts at box 20.
Answer: 14 boxes, starting at box 20

content.text:
Worked example: You sleep 8 hours on a weekday and 10 hours on a holiday. How many boxes of sleep does each strip have, and how many more on the holiday?
1. Each hour is 2 boxes.
2. Weekday: 8 × 2 = 16 boxes. Holiday: 10 × 2 = 20 boxes.
3. The holiday strip has 20 − 16 = 4 more boxes of sleep.
Answer: 16 boxes and 20 boxes; 4 more boxes, which is 2 more hours, on the holiday

The holiday strip has 20 − 16 = 4 more boxes of sleep.

content.text:
Data Story: Sleepy-Deepy. Isn't it amusing that there are animals that sleep as little as 2 hours per day and animals that sleep as much as 20 hours per day? Humans typically sleep for about 7 to 9 hours a day. The amount of sleep people need depends on age, living conditions, lifestyle among other factors.
The line graphs below show typical sleep durations of Indians across ages 6 to 75. The second picture is a zoomed-in version of the first picture. Share your observations on this graph.
Unlike the earlier graphs that were made up of a few connected line segments, this line graph looks like a smooth curve because it contains 80 data points that are placed very close to each other. Representing the same data using a column graph would require 70 columns, making the graph look cluttered and heavy.
From the graph we can see that the average sleep time for 6-year olds is about 9.5 hours per day. The daily sleep time decreases as we grow through teenage years and step into adulthood, touching about 8 hours a day between ages 30 and 50. After 50, the daily sleep time increases, reaching about 8.5 hours.
You might wonder why newborns and infants sleep for so long. Do people in different countries sleep differently? Do animals also exhibit such patterns in sleep durations across age?

2. Between ages 30 and 50 it reads about 8 hours.
3. 9.5 − 8 = 1.5 hours more.
Answer: About 1.5 hours more a day

media.title: Data Project Workspace
media.context: Class 8 NCERT Ganita Prakash Part II ch 5 'Tales by Dots and Lines' (plan chapter 12, Your Own Data Story). Pick a project, enter data, and find the mean and median. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student opens an empty project workspace. A question box sits at the top, below it a data table with a row for each day or each person, and beside it automatic read-outs for the mean and the median. A switch chooses a strip or a line graph, a comparison column waits for an adult's or a group's data, and a findings note is at the bottom.

The workspace begins with the question, not the data. The student writes a question, such as how long the family sleeps, and a guess, such as whether children, adults and the elderly sleep the same. The graph stays closed until both are written. Then the student chooses what to record, for whom and for how many days, and picks one of two projects: a week of family sleep, or the daily timings of Grade 8 schools. Card 1 asks the student to enter seven days of sleep and read the mean and the median. If the two differ, the tool says why. For 9, 8.5, 10 and 9 hours the mean is about 9.1 and the median 9, because the 10 pulls the mean up a little.

Card 2 asks the student to show the data on a strip or a line graph, whichever suits it, with the 30 minute boxes on a strip counting hours. For example, 1.5 hours outdoors is 3 boxes. Card 3 adds an adult's data in the comparison column, so the student can set the two side by side and say what is similar and what is different. Card 4 pools a group's sleep data by age group, children, adults and elderly, and shows a mean and median for each. Card 5 collects school timings. A school day of 9:30 am to 4:30 pm is 7 hours with class time and breaks, and the student averages the days of several schools. Card 6 asks for a finding and a new question. A finding that the data does not support is flagged with the values, and the note cannot be saved without a question.

Hints go in order: what question do you want your data to answer? Then: decide what to record, for whom and for how many days. Then: enter the values, then compare the mean with the median. Last, a sample entry and graph are shown to start and the student continues with their own data. Through doing, the student learns the whole path of an investigation: ask, collect, summarise with a mean and median, show in a graph, say what was found, and end with a new question.

content.text:
Individual project: Make your own activity strip for different days of the week.
Do you eat and sleep at regular times every day? Typically how long do you spend outdoors?
Calculate the average time spent per activity. Represent this average day using a strip.
Similarly, track the activities of any adult at home. Compare your data with theirs.

1. Predict first: do you eat and sleep at the same time every day? Write your guess before you collect any data.
2. Record each activity for several days. For each activity, add the times and divide by the number of days to get the average. Colour an average day on a strip.
3. Track an adult at home the same way and compare the two strips.

content.text:
Worked example: Over 3 days you spend 1.5 hours, 2 hours and 1 hour outdoors. What is the average time outdoors, and how many boxes is it on a strip?
1. Add the three days: 1.5 + 2 + 1 = 4.5 hours.
2. Divide by 3: 4.5 ÷ 3 = 1.5 hours.
3. Each hour is 2 boxes, so 1.5 × 2 = 3 boxes.
Answer: 1.5 hours a day, which is 3 boxes on the strip

content.text:
Small group project: Make a group of 3 to 4 members. Do at least one of the following:
Track daily sleep time of all your family members for a week. Daily sleep time includes night sleep, naps, and any sleep during the day. Represent this on strips. Put together the data of all your group members. Calculate the average and median sleep time of children, adults, elderly. Share your findings and observations.

content.text:
Worked example: Four children in a group sleep 9, 8.5, 10 and 9 hours. Find the mean and the median sleep time.
1. Mean: 9 + 8.5 + 10 + 9 = 36.5, and 36.5 ÷ 4 = 9.125 hours.
2. Median: in order 8.5, 9, 9, 10; the middle two are 9 and 9.
3. (9 + 9) ÷ 2 = 9 hours.
Answer: Mean about 9.1 hours, median 9 hours

content.text:
Last year we looked at mean as a fair-share. Here, we learnt how the sum of the distances of the values to its left and right are the same.
We saw that when values greater than the mean are inserted, the mean increases. When values less than the mean are inserted, the mean decreases. Similar phenomena can be observed with the median.
Line graphs can be used to visualise change over time.
We saw that examining data can lead to new questions and directions to probe further.

content.text:
1. Our opening guess is settled: the mean of two numbers sits halfway between them, and for any data the distances on the two sides of the mean add up to the same total.
2. A value above the mean pulls the mean up, a value below pulls it down, and the median moves only when the middle moves.
3. Line graphs follow change over time. Still open for you: pick one graph from this chapter and write two questions it raises.

content.text: Game of Hex. Hex is a two-player strategy game played on a rhombus-shaped board made of hexagonal cells, usually of size 11 × 11. Each player is assigned a colour and two opposite sides of the board. Players take turns placing a piece of their colour on any empty cell. Once placed, pieces can not be moved or removed. The objective is to create an unbroken chain of one's own pieces connecting the two assigned sides. The first player to complete such a connection wins the game.

3. Play with a partner on paper and talk about the moves that helped.

content.text:
Worked example: On a 3 by 3 Hex board the players fill all 9 cells. Can the game end with neither player joining their two sides?
1. Try filling a small board in every way you can: one colour always joins its two sides.
2. A wall of one colour that blocks the other side is itself a chain across the board.
3. So a full board always has exactly one winner.
Answer: No; a Hex game can never end in a draw

Students place cities on a map of India, switch their rainfall lines on and off, mark peak and low months, and group the cities by when they get their rain.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students read the colour scale that maps the difference between rice and wheat eating from minus 100 to plus 100, and explain what a value of plus 100 means.
Students list the five states most preferring rice and wheat, name some balanced states, and estimate the hidden value for Karnataka from the values of its neighbours.
Students tap states to read their values, rank the top five on each side, drag a threshold to find balanced states, and place a guess for a hidden state before it is revealed.
Students match colours to activities with the key, work out the time of an activity from the box count, and infer which day of the week a strip shows and when a long movie happened.
Students sketch how their own weekday strip and a holiday strip would look, and compare them with an adult's strip, naming what is similar and different.
Students read a smooth line graph of sleep time over age, say why 80 points look like a curve, and compare the full graph with the zoomed one.
Students colour the 48 boxes of a strip with a key, read off the hours spent on each activity, and compare two strips box by box.
Students choose a question about their own day, decide what to record and for how many days, and describe how they will summarise and show the data.
Students choose one group investigation, either a week of family sleep or the daily timings of Grade 8 schools, and decide how to combine the data of all members using the mean and median.
Students enter their own day's data, see the mean, the median and a strip or graph update, compare with an adult or a group, and write findings and new questions.

Students restate that the mean balances distances on both sides, how adding values changes the mean and median, that line graphs show change over time, and that data leads to new questions.
